title: Character.AI has filed for bankruptcy. Here is what happens to the app
subtitle: The AI character chat app is up for sale, and Disney has bid $20 million for some of its tech. Explained in simple words.
content_html:
Picture this. You open an app and chat with an AI version of your favourite anime hero, or a character you made up yourself. For a few years, millions of people did exactly that on Character.AI.

Now the company behind it is in deep trouble. On October 12, 2026, it filed for bankruptcy in a US court in Delaware. It also agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million.

So will the app shut down? What is Disney getting? Let us break it down.

First, what is Character.AI?

Character.AI is an app where you can create AI characters and chat with them. Two former Google engineers, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, started it in late 2021.

It grew fast. By October 2024, it had 20 million monthly active users. That means 20 million different people opened it at least once in a month. Sensor Tower, a firm that tracks apps, ranked it among the top apps by time spent.

In this older interview, co-founder Noam Shazeer talks about how the team built the app and grew it to 20 million users.

What does bankruptcy mean?

Bankruptcy is what a company does when it is in serious money trouble and asks a court for help.

In the US, there are different kinds. Character.AI filed for Chapter 11. Chapter 11 does not mean the company shuts the next morning. It gives the company time and some protection while a court watches over it.

Think of the court as the umpire in a cricket match. It makes sure everyone follows the rules, including the people the company owes money to.

During the sale, the company says it will keep running the app with "minimal service disruptions". So for now, the app still works.

What is Disney getting for $20 million?

Disney is not buying the whole app. Its bid covers some assets, including a licence to use some of Character.AI's technology forever.

A licence is permission to use something you do not own. It is like paying to use a friend's cricket bat for every match, while the bat still belongs to your friend. This licence is also non-exclusive. That means others can get permission to use the same tech too.

Disney is what lawyers call the "stalking horse" bidder. It is a funny name for a simple idea. Disney's offer sets the starting price, like the base price for a player at an IPL auction. Other buyers can now come in and bid higher.

The sale is expected to finish by late November or early December 2026.

There is a twist. Last month, some former Character.AI employees and former CEO Karandeep Singh Anand joined Disney. Now they will help with the handover.

Will the app shut down?

Maybe. It depends on who buys it.

The company's CEO, Colin Adams, said the board decided that this court-run sale gives the company "the best opportunity" to get the most value. If a buyer wants to keep the app going, it lives on. If no such offer comes, he said, "the platform will be wound down". Wound down is a polite way of saying it will be closed, step by step.

A court filing lists the company's assets at between $50 million and $100 million. Assets are things a company owns, like cash and technology. Its liabilities, the money it owes, fall in the same range.

How did a hit app end up here?

Back in 2024, Google signed a $2.7 billion deal to license Character.AI's models. After that, both founders went back to Google. Character.AI then stopped building its own big AI models and focused on growing the app.

Compare that $2.7 billion with Disney's $20 million bid now. The new number is 135 times smaller. The two deals are not the same kind of deal, but the gap is huge.

TechCrunch points to two big problems:

  • Legal trouble. The company faced lawsuits and an investigation in Texas over child safety. In January 2026, it settled some of the lawsuits, added safety features, and stopped minors from using the app.
  • AI is costly to run. Every chat runs on powerful computers, and those cost money. So the more people chat, the bigger the bill. Imagine a chai stall where every cup you pour costs you money. More customers means a bigger bill, unless they pay enough for each cup.

The company tried new ideas, like AI videos, social feeds and short interactive stories. But TechCrunch says these changes did not make the business strong enough.

Investors had put in more than $193 million, from firms such as a16z and Lightspeed, according to PitchBook data quoted by TechCrunch.

What this means for app users

This story is a good reminder. Even a free app costs money to run. When a company cannot pay its bills, the app people love can get a new owner, or disappear.

For now, Character.AI is still running. The next few weeks will decide what happens to it.
